In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.$ Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}x(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x){cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}x{sec}^{2}⁡x{cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}x\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}-0) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$
